bib.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning with Diff Pruning

question: Can a task-specific sparse difference vector added to frozen pretrained weights match full finetuning while storing far fewer parameters per task?
hypothesis: A diff vector regularised with a differentiable L0 relaxation can be very sparse (about 0.5%) with little loss versus full finetuning, and structured grouping helps further.
contributions: Diff pruning: theta_task = theta_pretrained + delta_task with delta sparsified via relaxed L0 penalty
Magnitude-pruning projection onto an L0 ball for exact sparsity, followed by fixed-mask finetuning
Structured variant with a per-group mask (393 groups)
Matches full finetuning on GLUE at 0.5% new params per task; beats compression methods on storage

method.summary: Reparameterise task parameters as theta + delta with theta frozen; delta = z * w where z is a stretched Hard-Concrete relaxed binary mask with an expected-L0 penalty. After training, magnitude-prune delta to a target sparsity and finetune with the mask fixed. Structured version multiplies a per-group scalar mask.
method.task: Transfer learning on GLUE classification/regression tasks and SQuAD v1.1 extractive QA

datasets.name: GLUE (MNLI, QQP, QNLI, SST-2, CoLA, STS-B, MRPC, RTE)
datasets.split: test server for Table 1; validation set for analysis

models.name: Diff pruning / structured diff pruning
models.params: inferred: 0.5% of base parameters nonzero per task
models.init_from: pretrained BERT; w init 0, alpha init 5

training.objective: cross-entropy plus lambda * expected L0 norm of delta; then fixed-mask finetuning after magnitude pruning
training.lr: GLUE per task 1e-5 to 5e-5 (Table 7); fixed-mask phase 5e-5; SQuAD 3e-5
training.batch_size: GLUE 8 (12 for STS-B); SQuAD per-GPU 3 on 8 GPUs
training.epochs: GLUE: 3 initial + 3 fixed-mask (5 for MRPC/STS-B/RTE/SST-2); SQuAD 2 + 2
training.regularisation: relaxed L0 penalty lambda=1.25e-7; Hard-Concrete l=-1.5, r=1.5
training.wall_clock: 1.5x to 2x slower per minibatch than regular finetuning
training.seeds: Fig 3 shows 5 runs of SST-2; main-table seed count not stated

other.search: batch size in {5,8,12,16}, lr in {1e-5,2e-5,5e-5}, selected on validation
other.sampling: u sampled once to get z at end of training
other.table7: lr QNLI 2e-5, SST-2 5e-5, MNLI 1e-5, CoLA 1e-5, MRPC 1e-5, STS-B 1e-5, RTE 1e-5, QQP 2e-5

results.claim: Training is 1.5x to 2x slower per minibatch than regular finetuning, and needs more memory for alpha and w.
Modifying only the FC layers after self-attention (adapter-like placement) gave much worse performance, suggesting adapters' restricted read/write points limit efficiency.
results.setup: footnote 15, diff pruning restricted to FC layers after self-attention

limits: Training needs more memory than usual finetuning (also optimises alpha and w) and is 1.5-2x slower per minibatch; the authors flag this as a concern as models grow.
Storing the diff needs nonzero positions as well as weights.
No inference speedup, unlike compression methods (TinyBERT4 is 9.4x faster).
Only BERT-large/base evaluated in main experiments; RoBERTa and XLNet only in preliminary unreported runs.
Only encoder models and GLUE/SQuAD; no generative LLM; storage is a basic Python estimate.
Adapters numbers are copied from Houlsby et al., and QNLI is not directly comparable.
Seed variance for main results not reported; Fig 3 shows nontrivial variation in which layers are modified.
The 'regularization effect' on SQuAD is a conjecture, not tested.

code.snippet: u ~ U(0,1); s = sigmoid(log u - log(1-u) + alpha); s_bar = s*(r-l)+l; z = min(1, max(0, s_bar)); delta = z (.) w
